lead: After the Passover night comes the departure. The first reading tells of Israel marching out of Egypt with unleavened dough on their backs, and calls the night a vigil kept for the Lord for all generations. In the Gospel the Pharisees plot against Jesus after the sabbath healing, and he quietly withdraws, healing all who follow him. Matthew sees in this gentleness the Servant of Isaiah, who will not break a bruised reed or quench a smoldering wick. Both readings show God’s way of saving: not with noise and force of arms, but in a night of watching and in a quiet service of the weak.

set: Yesterday’s reading (Exodus 11:10–12:14) gave the instructions for the Passover; today’s tells of the departure itself. The night of the tenth plague has passed, and Pharaoh has let Israel go (12:29–32). The people leave in haste from Rameses, the royal city in the eastern delta, and make their first stop at Succoth. The passage is a short narrative summary, written with a liturgical tone, and its last verse turns from the past to the feast kept for ever.
str: v. 37: the march from Rameses to Succoth, with six hundred thousand men on foot, besides children.
v. 38: a mixed crowd and great flocks and herds go with them.
v. 39: unleavened cakes baked from the dough, because there was no time to prepare.
vv. 40–41: the time in Egypt: four hundred and thirty years, ending exactly on that day.
v. 42: it was a night of vigil for the Lord, to be kept by all the Israelites for ever.
kw: Other peoples, probably slaves and poor workers of different origins, joined Israel in its going out. The people of God has always been open to those who attach themselves to it (compare Exodus 12:48–49).
Bread made without yeast, because there was no time to wait for it to rise. Israel keeps this bread each year as a reminder of the haste of the deliverance.
Literally “a night of keeping” or “watching”. God kept watch to bring them out, and Israel is to keep watch in return. The word suggests both God’s care and the people’s attention.
vv: about six hundred thousand men on foot, besides children.

The number is very large, and scholars debate how to understand it (some think the Hebrew word translated “thousand” may also mean a clan or military unit). What the verse says for sure is that the whole people went out, as one people.
A mixed crowd also went up with them,
From the very beginning those who join Israel are among the people God leads out. Salvation is not shut to any who come with them.
because they were driven out of Egypt and could not wait,
The people did not plan their own liberation. God’s act came suddenly, and they had to follow.
That was for the Lord a night of vigil, to bring them out of the land of Egypt.
The night of the exodus is a night when God was watching over his people, and every year those who keep it watch with him.
ch: The Church remembers this night every year at the Easter Vigil, the “mother of all vigils”, which begins in the dark and reads the story of the exodus. The Exsultet, the great proclamation of Easter, sings in substance that this is the night when God first saved our fathers and delivered the children of Israel from slavery in Egypt. The Church reads the Passover as the great type of Christ’s own passing from death to life, and it also honors the Jewish people who have kept the vigil of Passover through every century. Paul recalls the 430 years when he explains that the promise to Abraham came long before the law (Galatians 3:17).

r.h: He will not break a bruised reed
set: The passage follows the sabbath healing of the man with the withered hand (12:9–13). Some Pharisees are angered and plan how to destroy Jesus. The Pharisees were a lay movement of devout Jews; Matthew names those in this scene, not the whole group and certainly not the Jewish people. Jesus does not answer with a counter-attack. He withdraws, and he goes on healing, and Matthew finds in this the first Servant Song of Isaiah (Isaiah 42:1–4).
str: v. 14: the plot of the Pharisees.
vv. 15–16: Jesus withdraws; the crowds follow; he heals them all and asks that he not be made known.
vv. 17–21: Matthew’s quotation of Isaiah 42:1–4: the chosen servant, filled with the Spirit, brings justice to the nations without quarrel or noise, and the Gentiles will hope in his name.
kw: The Greek word can mean both. It renders the Hebrew ʿebed, the servant who belongs to the Lord and does his will. At the baptism of Jesus the Father’s voice uses the same words of love (3:17).
The right order God brings to the world, especially in defense of the poor and the wronged. The servant brings it “to victory”, not by force but by faithful gentleness.
A reed already cracked, which any pressure would snap. The picture is of something weak and damaged, and the servant treats it with care.
vv: the Pharisees went out and conspired against him, how to destroy him.
The sabbath healing, an act of mercy, is the occasion of the plot. Here begins the road that leads to the Cross.
he cured all of them,
Jesus does not withdraw to rest alone. Even when he leaves the scene of conflict, he serves those who follow.
he ordered them not to make him known.
Jesus does not wish to be known first as a wonder-worker or as a political figure. He lets his mission unfold in its own way, as that of a servant who will suffer.
Here is my servant, whom I have chosen, my beloved,
The words recall the voice at the baptism, “This is my beloved Son” (3:17). Matthew shows that the Son is also the Servant.
He will not break a bruised reed or quench a smoldering wick until he brings justice to victory.
This is the heart of the passage: strength is shown in gentleness. Jesus will not crush those who are weak in faith or in strength.
in his name the Gentiles will hope.
The scene of conflict with some of his own people ends with a word of hope for the nations. Matthew’s Gospel, written for a community of Jewish and Gentile believers, holds both.
ch: The Catechism points to the Servant of Isaiah as one of the ways the Spirit prepared the coming of the Messiah (CCC 713). The Church sees in the bruised reed and smoldering wick the way Jesus meets sinners and the weak: he calls them, forgives them, and does not break them. Pastors and confessors are asked to imitate this gentleness. The Church recalls too that the Servant’s mission is to bring justice to the nations, which is why the Gospel is preached to all peoples.

qa: Does this Gospel say that the Pharisees as a group wanted to kill Jesus?

No. Matthew speaks of some Pharisees in this scene. In the Gospels other Pharisees invite Jesus to dinner and warn him of danger (Luke 7:36; 13:31), and Nicodemus and Joseph of Arimathea, who were of the leading class, honor him at the end. The Church teaches that what happened to Jesus in his Passion cannot be blamed on all the Jews of that time, nor on the Jews of today (Nostra Aetate 4).
study: The Israelites left Egypt in haste, with only dough and a mixed crowd. When has God asked me to move before I felt ready?
Jesus will not break a bruised reed. Whose weakness do I treat roughly, in my family or parish, and how could I treat it with his gentleness?
